beliefs.limiting: I’ve watched porn since I was a teenager. It’s wired in. I’m stuck with it.
beliefs.counterpart: Out-of-control porn use often doesn’t last. Plenty of people get past it.
beliefs.test: This week, write down one habit you were once sure you’d never drop, and did. Next to it, write what changed. Notice whether “wired in” held up.
beliefs.proof: An Israeli study checked adults for compulsive sex or problem porn use in 2018 and 2022. Of those flagged in 2018, 138 had recovered by 2022; 42 had not.

beliefs.limiting: Quitting means a brutal flatline and weeks of withdrawal.
beliefs.counterpart: I’ve had days off before. They weren’t brutal; the pull was the hard part.
beliefs.test: Rate your mood, sleep and focus 0–10 each night: three nights while you still watch, then each night of your first days off. Notice which nights score worse.
beliefs.proof: In a small study, 14 men who scored as hooked on sex or porn stopped all sex for 10 days. Their withdrawal-type symptoms eased from day 3 and by day 10 matched men who weren’t hooked.

refs.cite: Sassover E, Kushnir T, Weinstein AM (2024). Investigating mood-modification, withdrawal, and sensitization in compulsive sexual behaviour. Frontiers in Psychiatry 15:1421028. Study 3.
refs.quote: This study found that individuals with CSB experienced improvements in various symptoms after abstaining from sexual activity. That was evident as early as the 3rd day after abstention.

beliefs.limiting: I need it to switch off. Nothing else works at the end of the day.
beliefs.counterpart: Porn is one way I switch off. It isn’t the only one I have.
beliefs.test: The next three times you reach for porn to switch off, do something else for 15 minutes first: a walk, a shower, a call. Rate the pull 0–10 before and after. Notice how much of the need the swap covered.
beliefs.proof: In 104 men’s quit journals, most calling themselves addicted, porn had been how they handled bad moods, so bad moods became a trigger. Their own accounts, not a trial.

beliefs.limiting: I slipped again. I’m just someone who can’t quit.
beliefs.counterpart: A slip is one day. The days I kept still happened.
beliefs.test: If you slip this week, write down that night what came just before it. Then count the days you kept this month. Notice whether the slip deleted any of them.
beliefs.proof: Of 104 men journaling a porn quit, most calling themselves addicted, 55 slipped at least once. The researchers’ reading of the journals: quitting is hard, and achievable. Men’s own accounts, not a trial.

do: Write down what porn does for you: stress relief, sleep, boredom, loneliness.
Each one is a belief to test. Start with the table above.
Don’t quit yet. For the next few days, watch the way you normally do.
Before each time, write one line: the hour, where you are, what you felt just before.
After, one more line: what it gave you, and what it cost.
At the end, circle what repeats. Those hours and feelings are what your swaps are for.

proof.text: In a 10-week diary study of 9 men seeking help, binges came with low mood, stress or anxiety, and which one differed from man to man.

ref.cite: Wordecha M, Wilk M, Kowalewska E, Skorko M, Łapiński A, Gola M (2018). “Pornographic binges” as a key characteristic of males seeking treatment for compulsive sexual behaviors: qualitative and quantitative 10-week-long diary assessment. Journal of Behavioral Addictions 7:433-444.
ref.quote: diary assessment data indicate that specific correlates of binge PuM (decreased mood, increased stress, and anxiety) differ between subjects

do: Late nights: the phone charges outside the bedroom.
Stress or boredom: a walk, a workout, a call with a friend.
Loneliness: put that energy into meeting real people.
A craving that won’t let go: a cold shower, then out of the room.
The laptop lives on a desk or a shared table, never in bed.
A swap only has to cover 80% of the need. It doesn’t have to feel as good.

proof.text: Men journaling a porn quit, most calling themselves addicted, filled the gap with exercise, going out, meditating and better sleep. Their own accounts, not a trial.

ref.quote: Day-to-day behavioral strategies (e.g., exercising, meditating, socializing, keeping busy, going out more often, and having a healthier sleep routine) were incorporated as part of an overall lifestyle change

do: Install a blocker and give the password to someone else.
Start with a 7-day break as an experiment.
Put that first day a few days or weeks out, not tonight, and tell one person the date.
After the week, keep going: for three months, porn is the one thing. Leave the rest of your life as it is.
Mark every kept day. Each one is a complete success, whatever else went wrong.
Slip? Write down what came just before it, then go back to step 1.

proof.text: In 104 men’s quit journals, blockers helped somewhat; support from other people and being accountable to someone helped most. Their own accounts, not a trial.

ref.cite: Fernandez DP, Kuss DJ, Griffiths MD (2021). The pornography “rebooting” experience: a qualitative analysis of abstinence journals on an online pornography abstinence forum. Archives of Sexual Behavior 50:711-728.
ref.quote: blocking applications, was described to be somewhat useful. However, social support and accountability appeared to be the external resources that were most instrumental

do: If shame is the engine, work on your values, not only the habit.
A slip is information, not proof you’re broken.
When the urge comes, name it: “there is a craving.” Not “I want to.” Never “I need to.”
Don’t fight the thought. Let the craving sit there and carry on with what you were doing.
When it pulls, answer the way a man who doesn’t watch porn would: “I don’t watch that.”
Count the evenings you get back, not the days you missed.

proof.text: In men’s quit journals, pushing the thought of porn away was common, and some found over time that it backfired. Their own accounts, not a trial.

ref.cite: Fernandez DP, Kuss DJ, Griffiths MD (2021). The pornography “rebooting” experience: a qualitative analysis of abstinence journals on an online pornography abstinence forum. Archives of Sexual Behavior 50:711-728.
ref.quote: Attempting to suppress thoughts of pornography was a common cognitive strategy used, but some members realized over time that thought suppression was counterproductive

do: Look for a therapist who uses CBT or ACT.
Help is a tool for steps 1 to 4, not a replacement for them.
Embarrassed to ask? A therapist who works with this has heard it all before.
Try a group, online or in a room. Go a few times, and keep going only while it helps.
Don’t wait for a pill. None is proven for porn yet.

proof.text: In one small trial (28 men), viewing fell 93% after 12 sessions of ACT, against 21% on the waiting list.

ref.cite: Crosby JM, Twohig MP (2016). Acceptance and commitment therapy for problematic internet pornography use: a randomized trial. Behavior Therapy 47:355-366.
ref.quote: significant between-condition reductions in pornography viewing compared to the waitlist condition (93% reduction ACT vs. 21% waitlist)
